Chapter 4: The Intersection of Race, Gender, and Class
When we talk about race, it’s easy to focus on just that one part of someone’s identity. But honestly, life isn’t that simple, is it? Our experiences are shaped by a mix of things—race, gender, class—all working together in ways that can be pretty complicated.
Think about a young Black woman in Britain. Her experience isn’t the same as a Black man’s, or even a white woman’s. The way these identities overlap creates challenges that don’t fit into neat little boxes. Sometimes, it even leads to feeling left out from all sides.
Imagine this: you’re ambitious and outspoken, but you keep finding yourself caught between two worlds. In feminist spaces, if you bring up racism, you’re told it’s just a distraction from “real” women’s issues. But then, in anti-racist circles, your experiences as a woman can get pushed aside, too. It’s like you never fully belong anywhere.
That’s what intersectionality is really about. It’s the idea that our identities overlap in ways that can’t be separated, no matter how much society tries to split them apart.
Most people don’t even notice how the rules seem to change depending on who you are. A policy might look totally fair on paper, but for someone facing more than one kind of discrimination, the effects can be completely different.
Let’s look at the workplace for a second. Say you’re a Black woman aiming for a promotion. You might be passed over, not just because of your race, or just because you’re a woman, but because of the way those two identities combine. Maybe you’re seen as too assertive—or not assertive enough. Your achievements might get overlooked, and your mistakes stand out more than anyone else’s. And often, people who only see one piece of your identity just don’t notice the barriers you’re up against.
The same thing happens in the media. Stories about racism often focus on men, while stories about sexism zero in on white women. So what happens to everyone who doesn’t fit neatly into those categories? Their struggles just get ignored, and it’s like they’re invisible.
For a lot of people, realizing that their experiences aren’t being recognized can feel deeply isolating. It’s tough to push for change when you keep hearing that your problems don’t matter, or that you’re asking for too much. But you know what? That realization can also be a source of strength—a reminder that real justice means making space for everyone, not just those who fit the usual mold.
So here’s the real challenge: How do we build movements that actually see and honor these differences, instead of just smoothing them over? It’s not enough to talk about race, or gender, or class on their own. If we want real progress, we’ve got to have honest conversations about how all these forces interact—and commit to making sure everyone gets a seat at the table.
